claim: Misfolded proteins in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are retrotranslocated into the cytosol and polyubiquitinated before being degraded by the proteasome.
source: Misfolded proteins in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) are retrotranslocated into the cytosol and polyubiquitinated before being degraded by the proteasome.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the ERAD field, supported by citations in the introduction (Berner et al., 2018; Preston and Brodsky, 2017; Wu and Rapoport, 2018).

claim: The multi-spanning ubiquitin ligase Hrd1 forms the retrotranslocation channel.
source: The multi-spanning ubiquitin ligase Hrd1 forms the retrotranslocation channel and associates with three other membrane proteins (Hrd3, Usa1, Der1) of poorly defined function.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to structural and functional studies (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016; Schoebel et al., 2017) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Hrd1 associates with three other membrane proteins (Hrd3, Usa1, Der1).
source: The multi-spanning ubiquitin ligase Hrd1 forms the retrotranslocation channel and associates with three other membrane proteins (Hrd3, Usa1, Der1) of poorly defined function.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Carvalho et al., 2006; Denic et al., 2006; Gardner et al., 2000) in the introduction.

claim: The Hrd1 channel is gated by autoubiquitination.
source: The Hrd1 channel is gated by autoubiquitination, but how Hrd1 escapes degradation by the proteasome and returns to its inactive ground state is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016) cited in the introduction.

claim: Autoubiquitination of Hrd1 is counteracted by Ubp1, a deubiquitinating enzyme.
source: Here, we show that autoubiquitination of Hrd1 is counteracted by Ubp1, a deubiquitinating enzyme that requires its N-terminal transmembrane segment for activity towards Hrd1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ubp1 requires its N-terminal transmembrane segment for activity towards Hrd1.
source: Here, we show that autoubiquitination of Hrd1 is counteracted by Ubp1, a deubiquitinating enzyme that requires its N-terminal transmembrane segment for activity towards Hrd1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 2 showing that Ubp1 lacking the transmembrane segment (Ubp1 ΔTM) does not stabilize Hrd1.

claim: Hrd3 serves as a brake for autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
source: The Hrd1 partner Hrd3 serves as a brake for autoubiquitination, while Usa1 attenuates Ubp1's deubiquitination activity through an inhibitory effect of its UBL domain.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that deletion of Hrd3 results in excessive Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation (Figure 1B-C, Figure 3E).

claim: Usa1 attenuates Ubp1's deubiquitination activity through an inhibitory effect of its UBL domain.
source: The Hrd1 partner Hrd3 serves as a brake for autoubiquitination, while Usa1 attenuates Ubp1's deubiquitination activity through an inhibitory effect of its UBL domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 4 showing that Usa1 ΔUBL stabilizes Hrd1 more than wild-type Usa1.

claim: The Hrd1 channel is regulated by cycles of autoubiquitination and deubiquitination.
source: These results lead to a model in which the Hrd1 channel is regulated by cycles of autoubiquitination and deubiquitination, reactions that are modulated by the other components of the Hrd1 complex.
evidence: This is the central model proposed based on the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: S. cerevisiae substrates use four distinct ERAD pathways depending on the localization of their misfolded domains.
source: Work in S. cerevisiae showed that substrates use four distinct ERAD pathways, depending on the localization of their misfolded domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations (Carvalho et al., 2006; Foresti et al., 2014; Huyer et al., 2004; Khmelinskii et al., 2014; Vashist and Ng, 2004).

claim: ERAD-L substrates contain misfolded domains in the ER lumen.
source: ERAD-L substrates contain misfolded domains in the ER lumen, ERAD-M substrates are misfolded within the membrane, ERAD-C substrates are membrane proteins with misfolded cytosolic domains, and ERAD-INM handles misfolded proteins in the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in the ERAD field.

claim: ERAD-L and ERAD-M pathways use the Hrd1 ligase.
source: These pathways use different ubiquitin ligases: ERAD-L and -M use the Hrd1 ligase, ERAD-C the Doa10 ligase, and ERAD-INM the Asi ligase complex (Carvalho et al., 2006; Foresti et al., 2014; Huyer et al., 2004; Khmelinskii et al., 2014; Vashist and Ng, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Cdc48 ATPase cooperates with a cofactor (Ufd1/Npl4) to extract polyubiquitinated substrates from the membrane.
source: This ATPase cooperates with a cofactor (Ufd1/Npl4) to extract polyubiquitinated substrates from the membrane (Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stein et al., 2014.

claim: Hrd1 forms a complex with three other membrane proteins (Hrd3, Usa1, Der1).
source: Hrd1 forms a complex with three other membrane proteins (Hrd3, Usa1, Der1) (Carvalho et al., 2006; Denic et al., 2006; Gardner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hrd3 is a single-spanning membrane protein with a large lumenal domain that interacts with substrates and Hrd1.
source: Hrd3 is a single-spanning membrane protein with a large lumenal domain that interacts with substrates and Hrd1 (Gauss et al., 2006a; Gauss et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gauss et al., 2006a and 2006b.

claim: In the absence of Hrd3, Hrd1 is strongly autoubiquitinated and rapidly degraded.
source: In the absence of Hrd3, Hrd1 is strongly autoubiquitinated and rapidly degraded (Gardner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2000 and confirmed by data in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Usa1 is a double-spanning membrane protein that serves as a linker between Hrd1 and Der1.
source: Usa1 is a double-spanning membrane protein that serves as a linker between Hrd1 and Der1 and facilitates the oligomerization of Hrd1 (Carvalho et al., 2010; Horn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carvalho et al., 2010 and Horn et al., 2009.

claim: The UBL domain of Usa1 is dispensable for the degradation of ERAD substrates.
source: It also has a ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of poorly defined function; the UBL domain is dispensable for the degradation of ERAD substrates, but is required for the efficient degradation of Hrd1 in a hrd3Δ strain (Carroll and Hampton, 2010; Vashistha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroll and Hampton, 2010 and Vashistha et al., 2016.

claim: The UBL domain of Usa1 is required for the efficient degradation of Hrd1 in a hrd3Δ strain.
source: It also has a ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain of poorly defined function; the UBL domain is dispensable for the degradation of ERAD substrates, but is required for the efficient degradation of Hrd1 in a hrd3Δ strain (Carroll and Hampton, 2010; Vashistha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroll and Hampton, 2010 and Vashistha et al., 2016.

claim: Der1 is a multi-spanning protein required for ERAD-L, but not ERAD-M.
source: Der1 is a multi-spanning protein required for ERAD-L, but not ERAD-M; it probably recognizes misfolded substrates in the ER lumen and facilitates their insertion into Hrd1 (Knop et al., 1996; Mehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knop et al., 1996 and Mehnert et al., 2014.

claim: The Hrd1 ligase forms a protein-conducting channel.
source: Recent results suggest that the Hrd1 ligase forms a protein-conducting channel (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016.

claim: Overexpression of Hrd1 in S. cerevisiae cells bypasses the requirement for the other components of the complex.
source: Overexpression of Hrd1 in S. cerevisiae cells bypasses the requirement for the other components of the complex, while all downstream components, such as the ubiquitination machinery and Cdc48 ATPase complex, are still needed (Carvalho et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: The membrane-spanning segments of Hrd1 surround a deep aqueous cavity.
source: A cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure shows that the membrane-spanning segments of Hrd1 surround a deep aqueous cavity, supporting the idea that Hrd1 can form a channel (Schoebel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schoebel et al., 2017.

claim: Hrd1 reconstituted into proteoliposomes allows a misfolded substrate domain to retrotranslocate across the lipid bilayer.
source: In vitro experiments further demonstrate that Hrd1 reconstituted into proteoliposomes allows a misfolded substrate domain to retrotranslocate across the lipid bilayer (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016.

claim: Retrotranslocation by Hrd1 requires autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
source: This process requires autoubiquitination of Hrd1, leading to the suggestion that Hrd1 forms a ubiquitin-gated channel.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016.

claim: The important autoubiquitination event occurs in the RING finger domain of Hrd1.
source: The important autoubiquitination event occurs in the RING finger domain, as mutation of crucial lysines in this domain blocks retrotranslocation in vitro and ERAD-L in vivo (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016 and confirmed by data in Figure 3H-I.

claim: Hrd1 is autoubiquitinated in wild-type yeast cells.
source: Our previous experiments indicated that Hrd1 is autoubiquitinated in wild-type yeast cells (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in Figure 1F.

claim: Hrd1 has a half-life of about 100 min in wild-type yeast cells.
source: The protein is moderately stable, with a half-life of about 100 min.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from cycloheximide-chase experiments.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression causes the strongest increase of Hrd1 levels among 23 different DUBs tested.
source: The strongest increase of Hrd1 levels was seen with Ubp1, even though several other DUBs were expressed at a higher level than Ubp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression has no effect on the levels of Hrd3 or Usa1.
source: Ubp1 overexpression had no effect on the levels of Hrd3 or Usa1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: In hrd3Δ cells, Hrd1 has a half-life of about 30 min.
source: A more sensitive analysis of Ubp1 function can be performed with hrd3Δ cells, in which Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation are greatly accelerated (half-life of about 30 min).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from cycloheximide-chase experiments in Figure 1C.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression increases Hrd1 levels in hrd3Δ cells to about the same level as in wild-type cells.
source: Indeed, while Hrd1 levels are very low in hrd3Δ cells (Figure 1B; lane 3), Ubp1 overexpression increased Hrd1 to about the same level as in wild-type cells (Figure 1B; lane 8 versus 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: An enzymatically inactive mutant of Ubp1 (C110S) does not increase Hrd1 levels when overexpressed.
source: This increase was not seen when an enzymatically inactive mutant of Ubp1 (C110S) was overexpressed (Figure 1B, lane 13), indicating that the deubiquitination activity of Ubp1 is required for Hrd1 stabilization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: The deubiquitination activity of Ubp1 is required for Hrd1 stabilization.
source: This increase was not seen when an enzymatically inactive mutant of Ubp1 (C110S) was overexpressed (Figure 1B, lane 13), indicating that the deubiquitination activity of Ubp1 is required for Hrd1 stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of wild-type Ubp1 and Ubp1(C110S) effects on Hrd1 levels in Figure 1B.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression inhibits Hrd1 degradation in cells lacking Der1 or Usa1.
source: Overexpression of Ubp1 also inhibited Hrd1 degradation in cells lacking Der1 or Usa1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Wild-type Ubp1 has no effect on the degradation of enzymatically inactive Hrd1 mutant (C399S).
source: Furthermore, wild-type Ubp1 had no effect when co-expressed with an enzymatically inactive Hrd1 mutant (Figure 1D), indicating that Ubp1 reverses autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Ubp1 reverses autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
source: Furthermore, wild-type Ubp1 had no effect when co-expressed with an enzymatically inactive Hrd1 mutant (Figure 1D), indicating that Ubp1 reverses autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ubp1 has no effect on inactive Hrd1(C399S) in Figure 1D.

claim: Deletion of Ubp1 decreases the levels of Hrd1.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, the deletion of Ubp1, which should increase ubiquitination of Hrd1, decreased the levels of Hrd1 (Figure 1E; lanes 9–12 versus 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: The additional deletion of Hrd3 in ubp1Δ cells further reduces Hrd1 levels.
source: As expected, the additional deletion of the stabilizing Hrd1-partner Hrd3 further reduced Hrd1 levels (Figure 1E; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression reduces the level of polyubiquitinated Hrd1.
source: Indeed, the level of polyubiquitinated Hrd1 was reduced in wild-type or hrd3Δ cells overexpressing Ubp1, even though the levels of unmodified Hrd1 were increased (Figure 1F) and the total level of ubiquitinated proteins in the cell remained unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1F showing reduced ubiquitin signal on Hrd1 with Ubp1 overexpression.

claim: Hrd1 and Ubp1 interact in vivo.
source: To determine whether Hrd1 and Ubp1 interact in vivo, we performed co-immunoprecipitation experiments from yeast cells expressing Hrd1-Flag and Ubp1-V5. Indeed, a small, but reproducible amount of Hrd1-Flag was precipitated with antibodies to the V5 epitope (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1G.

claim: Ubp1 is 20-fold more abundant than Hrd1.
source: The low level of co-precipitation may be explained by the fact that Ubp1 is 20-fold more abundant than Hrd1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Ubp1-V5 does not precipitate Orm2-Flag.
source: The specificity of the interaction is supported by control experiments with Orm2, another integral membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum that is approximately 20 times more abundant than Hrd1: Ubp1-V5 did not precipitate Orm2-Flag (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1G showing no interaction between Ubp1 and Orm2.

claim: The interaction of Hrd1 with Ubp1 is maintained in the absence of Hrd3 or Usa1.
source: The interaction of Hrd1 with Ubp1 was maintained in the absence of Hrd3 or Usa1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: In the absence of Ubp1, CPY* degradation is slower than in cells expressing Ubp1.
source: In the absence of Ubp1 (Figure 1H, solid square with dashed black line), CPY* degradation was slower than in cells expressing Ubp1 (Figure 1H, circles with solid black line).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide-chase data in Figure 1H.

claim: Overexpression of Ubp1 does not prevent degradation of CPY*.
source: Importantly, overexpression of Ubp1 did not prevent degradation of CPY* (Figure 1H, triangles with red line) or the steady-state levels of CPY* (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ubp1 expression promotes the degradation of the overexpressed ERAD-L substrate GFP-CPY*.
source: The degradation of the overexpressed ERAD-L substrate, GFP-CPY* was also promoted by Ubp1 expression (in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Ubp1 is not required for ERAD-M.
source: Surprisingly, Ubp1 was not required for ERAD-M and overexpression of Ubp1 only slightly slowed degradation of ERAD-M substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Ubp1 promotes optimal ERAD-L, but not ERAD-M.
source: These data support the idea the Ubp1 is promoting optimal ERAD-L, but not ERAD-M.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Ubp1 on ERAD-L versus ERAD-M substrates shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ubp1 contains an N-terminal transmembrane segment followed by a cytosolic linker and catalytic domain.
source: Ubp1 contains an N-terminal transmembrane segment followed by a cytosolic linker and catalytic domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the schematic diagram in Figure 2A.

claim: Ubp1 is expressed as two distinct polypeptides, one with the transmembrane segment and one lacking it.
source: Ubp1 has been reported to be expressed as two distinct polypeptides; one with the transmembrane segment and the other lacking it (called ΔTM in the scheme in Figure 2A), generated from an internal translation start site (Met67) (Schmitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2005.

claim: Ubp1 lacking the transmembrane segment does not stabilize Hrd1 when overexpressed in hrd3Δ cells.
source: When Ubp1 lacking the transmembrane segment was overexpressed in hrd3Δ cells, no Hrd1 stabilization was observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: The transmembrane segment of full-length Ubp1 can be replaced by the unrelated transmembrane segment of the Cue4 protein.
source: However, the transmembrane segment of full-length Ubp1 could be replaced by the unrelated transmembrane segment of the Cue4 protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that TM(Cue4)Ubp1 stabilizes Hrd1.

claim: The role of the Ubp1 transmembrane segment is primarily to anchor Ubp1 at the ER membrane.
source: These results demonstrate that the role of the Ubp1 transmembrane segment is primarily to anchor Ubp1 at the ER membrane, which likely facilitates its interaction with the multi-spanning membrane protein Hrd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the Ubp1 TM can be replaced by an unrelated TM (Figure 2C).

claim: The membrane anchor of Ubp1 can be replaced by the Hrd1-interacting H-domain of Usa1.
source: In fact, the membrane anchor of Ubp1 could be replaced by the Hrd1-interacting H-domain of Usa1; this soluble fusion protein was able to completely stabilize Hrd1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that H-domain Ubp1 stabilizes Hrd1.

claim: Hrd1 stabilization is primarily achieved by H domain-dependent recruitment of the catalytic domain of Ubp1.
source: Together, these results suggest that Hrd1 stabilization is primarily achieved by H domain-dependent recruitment of the catalytic domain of Ubp1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H-domain Ubp1 fusion stabilizes Hrd1 (Figure 2C).

claim: Overexpression of the catalytic core of Usp2 has only a minor effect on Hrd1 stability.
source: Overexpression of the catalytic core of Usp2 had only a minor effect on Hrd1 stability (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: A fusion protein containing the transmembrane domain of Ubp1 followed by Usp2 has only a minor effect on Hrd1 stability.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fusion protein containing the transmembrane domain of Ubp1 followed by Usp2 (TM Usp2; Figure 2D), indicating that mere membrane targeting of the DUB is insufficient to stabilize Hrd1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: Mere membrane targeting of a DUB is insufficient to stabilize Hrd1.
source: Similar results were obtained with a fusion protein containing the transmembrane domain of Ubp1 followed by Usp2 (TM Usp2; Figure 2D), indicating that mere membrane targeting of the DUB is insufficient to stabilize Hrd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of TM Usp2 and H-domain Usp2 effects on Hrd1 stability in Figure 2D.

claim: Usp2 targeted directly to Hrd1 by the H domain of Usa1 stabilizes Hrd1.
source: However, stabilization was observed when Usp2 was targeted directly to Hrd1 by the Hrd1-interacting H domain of Usa1 (Figure 2D), even though this construct was expressed at a lower level than transmembrane Usp2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: Both wild-type Ubp1 and TM(Cue4)Ubp1 interact weakly with Hrd1.
source: Both wild-type Ubp1 and TM(Cue4)Ubp1 interacted weakly with Hrd1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: Ubp1 missing its transmembrane segment (Ubp1 ΔTM) does not interact with Hrd1.
source: In contrast, Ubp1 missing its transmembrane segment (Ubp1 ΔTM) did not interact with Hrd1 but a soluble version of Ubp1 carrying the H-domain of Usa1 showed strong interaction with Hrd1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: A soluble version of Ubp1 carrying the H-domain of Usa1 shows strong interaction with Hrd1.
source: In contrast, Ubp1 missing its transmembrane segment (Ubp1 ΔTM) did not interact with Hrd1 but a soluble version of Ubp1 carrying the H-domain of Usa1 showed strong interaction with Hrd1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a general correlation between Ubp1's Hrd1 interaction and its effect on Hrd1 stabilization.
source: Thus, there is a general correlation between Ubp1's Hrd1 interaction and its effect on Hrd1 stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the co-IP data in Figure 2E with the stabilization data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Wild-type Ubp1 is targeted to Hrd1 by both its transmembrane segment and the USP domain.
source: Together, these results suggest that wild-type Ubp1 is targeted to Hrd1 by both its transmembrane segment and the USP domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both the TM and the catalytic domain contribute to Hrd1 interaction and stabilization (Figure 2).

claim: The degradation of CPY* is drastically reduced when Hrd1, Usa1, Der1, or Hrd3 are absent.
source: As reported previously (Bordallo et al., 1998; Buschhorn et al., 2004; Carvalho et al., 2006; Denic et al., 2006; Knop et al., 1996), the degradation of CPY* was drastically reduced when either Hrd1, Usa1, Der1, or Hrd3 were absent (compare dashed lines in Figure 3A with those in Figure 3B–E), confirming that these components are all required for ERAD-L.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3A-E and supported by citations.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression rescues CPY* degradation in hrd3Δ cells.
source: Ubp1 overexpression only had an effect in hrd3Δ cells, where it rescued CPY* degradation (solid line in Figure 3E versus those in Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E.

claim: Hrd3's major function is to inhibit the ubiquitination activity of Hrd1.
source: These results suggest that Hrd3's major function is to inhibit the ubiquitination activity of Hrd1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ubp1 overexpression can bypass the requirement for Hrd3 in CPY* degradation (Figure 3E).

claim: Bypassing Hrd3 by Ubp1 overexpression does not obviate the need for the other ERAD-L components in CPY* degradation.
source: Importantly, bypassing Hrd3 by Ubp1 overexpression does not obviate the need for the other ERAD-L components in CPY* degradation (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3A-D showing that Ubp1 overexpression does not rescue CPY* degradation in hrd1Δ, usa1Δ, or der1Δ cells.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression stabilizes Hrd1 in hrd1Δhrd3Δ cells.
source: As expected from the results presented before, Ubp1 overexpression stabilized Hrd1 (Figure 3F) and allowed degradation of CPY* (Figure 3G), even in the absence of Hrd3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3F.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression allows degradation of CPY* in hrd1Δhrd3Δ cells expressing wild-type Hrd1.
source: As expected from the results presented before, Ubp1 overexpression stabilized Hrd1 (Figure 3F) and allowed degradation of CPY* (Figure 3G), even in the absence of Hrd3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3G.

claim: Hrd1 KRK mutant is stabilized by Ubp1 overexpression.
source: A Hrd1 mutant (Hrd1 KRK; Hrd1 with lysine to arginine substitutions at amino acids 319, 325, 366, 368, 370, 371, 373, 387, 407) that cannot be autoubiquitinated in its RING finger domain and is therefore inactive in retrotranslocation in vitro and in vivo (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016), was also stabilized by Ubp1 overexpression (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3H.

claim: Hrd1 KRK can still be polyubiquitinated in other domains.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the protein can still be polyubiquitinated in other domains (Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016; Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baldridge and Rapoport, 2016 and Stein et al., 2014.

claim: Higher Hrd1 KRK levels do not result in CPY* degradation.
source: However, as expected, the higher Hrd1 KRK levels did not result in CPY* degradation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3I.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression has little effect on the stability of catalytically inactive Hrd1(C399S).
source: Ubp1 overexpression had little effect on the stability of catalytically inactive Hrd1(C399S) (Figure 3J) or on the degradation of CPY* in Hrd1(C399S) expressing cells (Figure 3K), consistent with the notion that Ubp1 acts on polyubiquitinated Hrd1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3J.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression does not bypass normal Hrd1 function.
source: Because Ubp1 does not accelerate the degradation of CPY* in the presence of retrotranslocation-deficient Hrd1 KRK or inactive Hrd1(C399S) (Figure 3I and K), we conclude that Ubp1 overexpression does not bypass normal Hrd1 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ubp1 overexpression does not rescue CPY* degradation with inactive Hrd1 variants (Figure 3I, K).

claim: Stabilization of wild-type Hrd1 by Ubp1 overexpression results in the accelerated degradation of the ERAD-M substrate Erg3.
source: Stabilization of wild-type Hrd1 by Ubp1 overexpression also resulted in the accelerated degradation of the ERAD-M substrate Erg3 (Figure 3L) (Christiano et al., 2014; Jaenicke et al., 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3L.

claim: Hrd1 KRK variant is able to mediate the degradation of Erg3.
source: Surprisingly however, the Hrd1 KRK variant was also able to mediate the degradation of Erg3 (Figure 3M), in contrast to the ERAD-L substrate CPY* (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3M.

claim: Inactive Hrd1(C399S) is unable to support the degradation of Erg3.
source: Overexpression of Ubp1 did not bypass Hrd1 function because inactive Hrd1(C399S) was unable to support the degradation of Erg3 (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3N.

claim: Autoubiquitination of Hrd1 is not required for the degradation of the ERAD-M substrate Erg3.
source: It therefore appears that autoubiquitination of Hrd1 is not required for the degradation of this ERAD-M substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hrd1 KRK can mediate Erg3 degradation (Figure 3M).

claim: Usa1 is required for Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation in a hrd3Δ strain.
source: Previous reports demonstrated that Usa1 is required for Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation in a hrd3Δ strain (Carroll and Hampton, 2010; Vashistha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroll and Hampton, 2010 and Vashistha et al., 2016.

claim: The UBL domain of Usa1 is responsible for Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation in a hrd3Δ strain.
source: This activity could be assigned to the UBL domain of Usa1, but it remained unclear how this domain affects Hrd1 stability (Carroll and Hampton, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carroll and Hampton, 2010.

claim: Hrd1 is much more stable in hrd3Δusa1Δ strain than in a hrd3Δ single deletion strain.
source: To test this idea, we used a hrd3Δusa1Δ strain, in which Hrd1 is much more stable than in a hrd3Δ single deletion strain (Carroll and Hampton, 2010; see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and supported by citation to Carroll and Hampton, 2010.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type Ubp1 increases Hrd1 levels in hrd3Δusa1Δ strain.
source: Nevertheless, there was still some Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation in this strain, as overexpression of wild-type Ubp1, but not of enzymatically inactive Ubp1 (C110S), resulted in increased Hrd1 levels (Figure 4A, lanes 5–8 versus 9–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of Usa1 lacking its UBL domain (Usa1 ΔUBL) drastically stabilizes Hrd1 in hrd3Δusa1Δ strain.
source: Overexpression of Usa1 lacking its UBL domain (Usa1 ΔUBL) drastically stabilized Hrd1 (lanes 21–24), in contrast to wild-type Usa1, which only had a small effect on Hrd1 stability (lanes 17–20).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: The UBL domain of Usa1 attenuates Ubp1 activity.
source: Thus, the UBL domain of Usa1 indeed seems to attenuate Ubp1 activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Usa1 ΔUBL stabilizes Hrd1 more than wild-type Usa1 (Figure 4A).

claim: Co-overexpression of Usa1 and Ubp1 in hrd3Δ strain has little effect on Hrd1 levels compared to overexpression of Ubp1 alone.
source: The co-overexpression of Usa1 and Ubp1 in a hrd3Δ strain had little effect on Hrd1 levels and Hrd1 degradation compared to overexpression of Ubp1 alone (Figure 4B, lanes 5–8 versus 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-expression of Usa1 ΔUBL with Ubp1 strongly stabilizes Hrd1 in hrd3Δ strain.
source: However, when Usa1 ΔUBL was co-expressed with Ubp1, Hrd1 was strongly stabilized (lanes 9–12), indicating that the UBL domain of Usa1 indeed inhibits Ubp1 activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: In hrd3Δubp1Δusa1Δ triple-deletion mutant, Hrd1 is rapidly degraded.
source: In a triple-deletion mutant (hrd3Δubp1Δusa1Δ), Hrd1 was rapidly degraded (Figure 4C, lanes 1–4), but could be stabilized by its partner protein Hrd3 (lanes 5–8) or by increasing deubiquitination through Ubp1 overexpression (lanes 9–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: Usa1 or Usa1 ΔUBL have no effect on Hrd1 stability in the absence of Ubp1.
source: However, as expected from our model, Usa1 or Usa1 ΔUBL had no effect in the absence of Ubp1 (lanes 17–20 and 21–24).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of Usa1 ΔUBL causes stabilization of Hrd1 in hrd3Δubp1Δusa1Δ triple-deletion mutant when Ubp1 is expressed from its endogenous promoter.
source: When Ubp1 was expressed from its endogenous promoter in the triple-deletion mutant (hrd3Δubp1Δusa1Δ), the additional expression of Usa1 ΔUBL caused stabilization of Hrd1 (Figure 4D, lanes 9–12), whereas expression of wild-type Usa1 only had a small effect (Figure 4D, lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of Usa1 partially inhibits CPY* turnover.
source: Overexpression of Usa1 partially inhibited CPY* turnover (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, lanes 9–12 and Carvalho et al., 2010) and overexpression of Usa1 ΔUBL had a slightly stronger effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and supported by citation to Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: Degradation of ERAD-M substrates is unaffected by overexpressing Usa1 or Usa1 ΔUBL.
source: Degradation of these ERAD-M substrate still required Hrd1 but was unaffected by the overexpressing Usa1 or Usa1 ΔUBL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: ERAD-L is compromised by overexpressed Usa1 sequestering Der1.
source: The fact that overexpression of Usa1 and Usa1 ΔUBL disrupted ERAD-L, but not ERAD-M, suggests that ERAD-L was likely compromised by overexpressed Usa1 sequestering Der1 (Carvalho et al., 2010; Horn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on ERAD-L versus ERAD-M and supported by citations to Carvalho et al., 2010 and Horn et al., 2009.

claim: The UBL domain does not affect substrate degradation directly.
source: Taken together, these results support the idea that the UBL domain does not affect substrate degradation directly (Carroll and Hampton, 2010; Vashistha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carroll and Hampton, 2010 and Vashistha et al., 2016.

claim: Ubp1 is responsible for resetting polyubiquitinated Hrd1.
source: Our results now indicate that Ubp1, a membrane-bound DUB, is responsible for resetting Hrd1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ubp1 counteracts Hrd1's autoubiquitination and reduces its degradation.
source: Ubp1 counteracts Hrd1's autoubiquitination and therefore reduces its degradation (Figure 1B–F), while also regulating Hrd1's activity in ERAD-L (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1B-F, 1H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Ubp1 is an unusual DUB because it has an N-terminal transmembrane segment that is required for its activity towards Hrd1.
source: Ubp1 is an unusual DUB because it has an N-terminal transmembrane segment that is required for its activity towards Hrd1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: There are additional, unidentified determinants of specificity within the catalytic domain of Ubp1.
source: However, there seem to be additional, so far unidentified, determinants of specificity within the catalytic domain of Ubp1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Usp2 with the same membrane anchor does not stabilize Hrd1 as effectively as Ubp1 (Figure 2D).

claim: Substrate binding to Hrd3 releases the brake on Hrd1 autoubiquitination.
source: We propose that substrate binding to Hrd3 releases this brake (Figure 4E), allowing autoubiquitination of Hrd1, which in turn opens the channel for retrotranslocation of the substrate.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Hrd3 is not absolutely required for a basic ERAD process.
source: Hrd3 is not absolutely required for a basic ERAD process, as substrates are still degraded in its absence when Hrd1 is stabilized by Ubp1 overexpression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E and G.

claim: The ERAD-M substrate Erg3 does not require Hrd1 autoubiquitination or deubiquitination for its degradation.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the ERAD-M substrate Erg3 does not require Hrd1 autoubiquitination or deubiquitination for its degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3M showing that Hrd1 KRK can mediate Erg3 degradation.

claim: ERAD-M substrates might enter Hrd1 laterally with their transmembrane segments without requiring autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
source: ERAD-M substrates might enter Hrd1 laterally with their transmembrane segments and perhaps this does not require autoubiquitination of Hrd1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why ERAD-M substrates don't require Hrd1 autoubiquitination.

claim: ERAD-M (and ERAD-C) substrates may use the Der1 homolog Dfm1 for their extraction into the cytosol.
source: Alternatively, and more likely, ERAD-M (and ERAD-C) substrates may use the Der1 homolog Dfm1 for their extraction into the cytosol (Neal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Neal et al., 2018.

claim: Dfm1 mediates the cytosolic extraction of ERAD-M and ERAD-C substrates even in the absence of Hrd1 (or Doa10).
source: Dfm1 seems to mediate the cytosolic extraction of these ERAD substrates even in the absence of Hrd1 (or Doa10), which would explain why autoubiquitination and deubiquitination of Hrd1 is not required.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ERAD-M substrates don't require Hrd1 autoubiquitination and supported by citation to Neal et al., 2018.

claim: The presence of Ubp1 is required for optimal performance of ERAD-L.
source: The presence of Ubp1 is required for optimal performance of ERAD-L (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1H showing slower CPY* degradation in ubp1Δ cells.

claim: The decreased ERAD-L degradation rate in the absence of Ubp1 can be explained by decreased Hrd1 activity or enhanced Hrd1 degradation.
source: The decreased degradation rate in the absence of Ubp1 can be explained by decreased Hrd1 activity. Or alternately, decreased ERAD-L degradation could be explained by enhanced Hrd1 degradation caused by its insufficient deubiquitination.
evidence: These are alternative explanations for the observed effect of Ubp1 deletion on ERAD-L.

claim: The effect of Ubp1 deletion on ERAD-L is relatively small, perhaps because a combination of other DUBs can replace Ubp1.
source: The effect of Ubp1 deletion is relatively small, perhaps because a combination of other DUBs can replace Ubp1.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the modest effect of Ubp1 deletion.

claim: Overexpression of Ubp1 has no effect on the degradation of ERAD-L substrates.
source: The overexpression of Ubp1 has no effect on the degradation of ERAD-L substrates and slightly slows the degradation of ERAD-M substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Overexpression of Ubp1 slightly slows the degradation of ERAD-M substrates.
source: The overexpression of Ubp1 has no effect on the degradation of ERAD-L substrates and slightly slows the degradation of ERAD-M substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: ERAD-M substrates might be affected by Ubp1 overexpression because they are accessible to Ubp1 on the cytosolic side of the membrane prior to their extraction by Dfm1.
source: Perhaps, ERAD-M substrates are affected because they are accessible to Ubp1 on the cytosolic side of the membrane prior to their extraction from the membrane by Dfm1 (Neal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effect of Ubp1 overexpression on ERAD-M substrates, supported by citation to Neal et al., 2018.

claim: Deubiquitination of Hrd1 might reduce its activity towards ERAD-M substrates.
source: An alternate possibility is that deubiquitination of Hrd1 reduces its activity towards ERAD-M substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the effect of Ubp1 overexpression on ERAD-M substrates.

claim: The balance of Ubp1 activity could be advantageous for substrate specificity.
source: While Ubp1 does slow down the degradation rate of ERAD-M substrates, this balance could be advantageous for substrate specificity (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: The deletion of Hrd3 results in excessive Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation.
source: It has long been known that the deletion of Hrd3, which interacts with Hrd1 on the ER lumenal side, results in excessive Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation (Gardner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2000.

claim: Excessive Hrd1 autoubiquitination and degradation in hrd3Δ cells are attenuated when Usa1 or Usa1's UBL domain are also deleted.
source: These reactions were attenuated when Usa1 or Usa1's UBL domain were also deleted (Carroll and Hampton, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carroll and Hampton, 2010.

claim: In the absence of the UBL domain of Usa1, Ubp1 is hyperactive and reduces polyubiquitination of Hrd1 and its subsequent degradation.
source: Our results now explain these results by the demonstration that the UBL domain inhibits Ubp1. In the absence of this domain, Ubp1 is hyperactive and reduces polyubiquitination of Hrd1 and thus its subsequent degradation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is the explanation proposed based on the experimental findings in Figure 4.

claim: Functional interactions between UBL domains and DUBs have been reported, with DUBs being allosterically regulated or competitively inhibited by specific UBL domains.
source: However, functional interactions between UBL domains and DUBs have been reported, with DUBs being allosterically regulated or competitively inhibited by specific UBL domains (Faesen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Faesen et al., 2012.

claim: Although the absence of the UBL domain of Usa1 restored wild-type levels of Hrd1 in hrd3Δ cells, substrate degradation was still defective.
source: Although the absence of the UBL domain of Usa1 restored wild-type levels of Hrd1 in hrd3Δ cells, substrate degradation was still defective (Vashistha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vashistha et al., 2016.

claim: Both Hrd1 levels and ERAD can be restored in a hrd3Δ strain when Ubp1 is overexpressed.
source: Our experiments show that both Hrd1 levels and ERAD can be restored in a hrd3Δ strain when Ubp1 is overexpressed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3E and G.

claim: Hrd3 primarily performs a supporting role for Hrd1 through regulating Hrd1's autoubiquitination activity and helping to recruit ERAD substrates.
source: Thus, while Hrd3 is normally involved in ERAD, we suggest it primarily performs a supporting role for Hrd1 through regulating Hrd1's autoubiquitination activity and helping to recruit ERAD substrates (Carvalho et al., 2010; Gardner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to Carvalho et al., 2010 and Gardner et al., 2001.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression might still allow a low level of autoubiquitination that is sufficient for retrotranslocation, but not for efficient Hrd1 degradation.
source: In contrast, Ubp1 overexpression (in the presence of Usa1) might still allow a low level of autoubiquitination that is sufficient for retrotranslocation, but not for efficient Hrd1 degradation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Ubp1 overexpression does not completely overcome the inhibitory function of the UBL domain.
source: This interpretation implies that Ubp1 overexpression does not completely overcome the inhibitory function of the UBL domain, perhaps because the interaction between Hrd1 and Ubp1 is weak (Figure 1G) while that between Hrd1 and Usa1 is strong, or because Usa1 sterically prevents the access of Ubp1 to Hrd1 (Carvalho et al., 2006; Horn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Carvalho et al., 2006 and Horn et al., 2009.

claim: CPY* degradation is not accelerated by the increased Hrd1 levels caused by Ubp1 overexpression.
source: It is somewhat surprising that CPY* degradation is not accelerated by the increased Hrd1 levels caused by Ubp1 overexpression (Figures 1H and 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1H and 3A.

claim: Hrd1 functions in a complex with other components, including Hrd3, Usa1, and Der1, the levels of which remain unchanged with Ubp1 overexpression.
source: However, Hrd1 functions in a complex with other components, including Hrd3, Usa1, and Der1, the levels of which remain unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ubp1 does not act on polyubiquitinated ERAD-L substrate.
source: Importantly, overexpression of Ubp1 does not prevent the degradation of CPY* (Figures 1H and 3A), indicating that Ubp1 does not act on polyubiquitinated ERAD-L substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Ubp1 overexpression does not prevent CPY* degradation (Figures 1H and 3A).

claim: An ERAD substrate needs to retain its polyubiquitin chain until it has been extracted from the membrane by the Cdc48/p97 ATPase complex.
source: In fact, an ERAD substrate needs to retain its polyubiquitin chain until it has been extracted from the membrane by the Cdc48/p97 ATPase complex, because the polyubiquitin chain serves as a recognition signal for the Ufd1/Npl4 cofactor of Cdc48.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ERAD field.

claim: Substrate deubiquitination occurs by cytosolic DUBs, one of which is Otu1 (Yod1 in mammals).
source: Substrate deubiquitination occurs by cytosolic DUBs, one of which is Otu1 (Yod1 in mammals), an enzyme that binds to the Cdc48 ATPase through its UBX-like domain (Stein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stein et al., 2014.

claim: As long as the Cdc48 ATPase complex is bound to the membrane, Cdc48 interacts with Ubx2, which prevents access of Otu1.
source: As long as the ATPase complex is bound to the membrane, Cdc48 interacts with Ubx2, which prevents access of Otu1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bodnar and Rapoport, 2017; Ernst et al., 2009; Neal et al., 2017.

claim: Once Cdc48 has pulled the substrate out of the membrane and moved into the cytosol, Otu1 can trim the ubiquitin chain, the substrate is released from Cdc48/p97, and then transferred to the proteasome.
source: Once the ATPase has pulled the substrate out of the membrane and has moved into the cytosol, Otu1 can trim the ubiquitin chain, the substrate is released from Cdc48/p97, and then transferred to the proteasome (Bodnar and Rapoport, 2017; Ernst et al., 2009; Neal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bodnar and Rapoport, 2017; Ernst et al., 2009; Neal et al., 2017.

claim: ERAD involves two distinct deubiquitination reactions, one catalyzed by Ubp1 at the ER membrane to reset Hrd1, and another catalyzed by Otu1 in the cytosol to release substrate from Cdc48/p97.
source: Thus, ERAD involves two distinct deubiquitination reactions, one catalyzed by Ubp1 at the ER membrane to reset Hrd1, and another catalyzed by Otu1 in the cytosol to release substrate from Cdc48/p97.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and established knowledge.

claim: In both yeast and mammals, there are only two DUBs that are integral membrane proteins (out of 24 and 90 enzymes, respectively).
source: In both yeast and mammals, there are only two DUBs that are integral membrane proteins (out of 24 and 90 enzymes, respectively) (Komander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Komander et al., 2009.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Ubp1 is the only known DUB in the ER membrane.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Ubp1 is the only known DUB in the ER membrane (Schmitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2005.

claim: The N-terminal membrane anchor of Ubp1 is required for reversing the ubiquitin-modification of Hrd1 but can be replaced by a transmembrane segment from a different protein.
source: Our results show that the N-terminal membrane anchor is required for reversing the ubiquitin-modification of Hrd1 but that it can be replaced by a transmembrane segment from a different protein.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The apparent 20-fold excess of Ubp1 over Hrd1 makes it likely that Ubp1 has additional substrates which could contribute indirectly to Hrd1 stability.
source: The apparent 20-fold excess of Ubp1 over Hrd1 makes it is likely that Ubp1 has additional substrates which could contribute indirectly to Hrd1 stability.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the abundance data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A shorter version of Ubp1, which lacks the transmembrane segment, has been reported to have a role in endocytosis.
source: A shorter version of Ubp1, which lacks the transmembrane segment, has been reported to have a role in endocytosis (Schmitz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2005.

claim: Usp19 has been reported to serve as a DUB for polyubiquitinated Hrd1.
source: However, Usp19 has been reported to serve as a DUB for polyubiquitinated Hrd1 (Harada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harada et al., 2016.

claim: Usp19 is present at the ER membrane.
source: Usp19 is present at the ER membrane (Hassink et al., 2009), is proposed to play a role in ERAD (Lee et al., 2014), and is one of two mammalian DUBs with transmembrane segments (Komander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hassink et al., 2009.

claim: Usp19 is proposed to play a role in ERAD.
source: Usp19 is present at the ER membrane (Hassink et al., 2009), is proposed to play a role in ERAD (Lee et al., 2014), and is one of two mammalian DUBs with transmembrane segments (Komander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014.

claim: Usp19 is one of two mammalian DUBs with transmembrane segments.
source: Usp19 is present at the ER membrane (Hassink et al., 2009), is proposed to play a role in ERAD (Lee et al., 2014), and is one of two mammalian DUBs with transmembrane segments (Komander et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Komander et al., 2009.

claim: Mammalian Hrd1 is associated with HERP, a putative Usa1 homolog with a UBL domain.
source: Mammalian Hrd1 is associated with HERP (Schulze et al., 2005), a putative Usa1 homolog with a UBL domain (Kokame et al., 2000), but whether Usp19 functions in a similar way as Ubp1 in yeast remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulze et al., 2005 and Kokame et al., 2000.
